node.subject: double-sided tape creep and residue in fixturing
node.main_point: Using double-sided/carpet tape for temporary wood fixturing can creep under continuous load, particularly in warm conditions, and may leave adhesive residue on the workpiece.
node.source_quote: Many people have relied on types of double-sided tape, carpet tape being particularly favoured for its strong hold, for this sort of job for many years, but the hold can tend to creep with continual strain especially during warmer weather. And as you also mention it can leave a bothersome residue on the wood.
node.example_context: Woodworking workholding using double-sided/carpet tape

node.subject: adhesive layer thickness and creep (tape + CA method)
node.main_point: Masking tape avoids residue on wood, and because the CA glue layer in the tape-to-tape method is very thin, the joint is less prone to creep under load.
node.source_quote: Masking tape is of course purpose-made not to leave residue and the thinner glue layer means it's less subject to creep.
node.example_context: Woodworking temporary bonding using masking tape and CA glue

node.subject: masking tape and CA fixturing method
node.main_point: To create a rigid, low-profile temporary bond between two wood pieces for machining, apply masking tape to both mating faces and bond the tape layers together with CA (superglue).
node.source_quote: What you do is put tape on both pieces and simply superglue the tape together.
node.example_context: Woodworking temporary workholding for guiding parts through a saw/router

node.subject: performance of tape-to-tape CA joint
node.main_point: A tape-to-tape CA bond provides a strong, rigid hold during machining, yet the parts can be separated with light prying and the masking tape removes cleanly afterward.
node.source_quote: And the hold of the superglue is very strong and rigid, but despite this you can pop the two pieces apart with minimal prying. The masking tape then peels from the wood with ease.
node.example_context: Woodworking temporary fixturing with masking tape and CA glue

node.subject: assembly method and materials for laminated cores
node.main_point: For assembling a laminated stator/transformer core, varnish can both insulate and bond, but a preferable method is to use waxed paper between laminations, mechanically clamp the stack, and then encapsulate it with epoxy or varnish.
node.source_quote: Varnish would work for both insulating and bonding to a certain extent, but better would be waxed paper, then mechanically clamp it all together, and encapsulate the whole thing in epoxy or varnish afterwards.
node.example_context: DIY fabrication of laminated steel cores for motors/transformers

node.subject: vacuum hold-down using holes in fixture pocket
node.main_point: If your workpiece sits in a pocket, you can add holes through the pocket’s base and attach a vacuum source (like a vacuum cleaner) to hold the part down instead of using mechanical clamps or tape.
node.source_quote: As you have the "pocket" already, one method would be to have holes in the pocket base and use a vacuum cleaner to "suck" the piece down.
node.example_value: Use the existing pocket and connect a household vacuum cleaner to holes in the pocket base to pull the wooden piece down during milling.
node.example_context: CNC milling small wood parts located in a pocket; using a vacuum cleaner as the vacuum source for hold-down.

node.subject: thermal expansion effect on reamed hole size (cooled workpiece)
node.main_point: Reaming a hole while the workpiece is cold (with a room‑temperature reamer) will yield a final hole that ends up larger at room temperature, because the material expands as it warms after machining.
node.source_quote: If you cool the workpiece and the reamer is at "normal" temperature then your final hole will be larger.

node.subject: double-stick tape workholding and heat-assisted release for CFRP
node.main_point: Double‑stick carpet tape is a common way to hold small carbon‑fiber composite parts; releasing the tape may require heat, which the composite can tolerate provided the epoxy is not overheated.
node.source_quote: Double stick carpet tape is a common substance and may require heating to remove without breaking the part, but carbon fiber composite can handle temperatures well enough as long as the epoxy resin is not damaged.
node.example_context: Workholding thin carbon‑fiber composite parts on a sacrificial board

node.subject: minimum feature size DRC in planar mill CAM
node.main_point: Planar-milling CAM software typically includes a minimum feature-size design rule check that can automatically remove thin copper slivers. Using this DRC can prevent leftover shavings during PCB milling.
node.source_quote: Any good planar mill CAM program will have a design rule check for minimum feature size, and should be able to remove such slivers automatically. Worth checking into it.
node.example_context: planar mill CAM for PCB isolation routing

node.subject: epoxy filler adhesion vs removability tradeoff
node.main_point: Using epoxy or similar resins as a temporary filler presents a tradeoff: if they adhere well, removal is difficult; if a release agent is used, they won’t adhere and must be mechanically retained.
node.source_quote: The problem with epoxies or similar resins is that it will either adhere and be hard to remove or id you use a release agent it won't adhere at all unless it is held in by other means.

node.subject: residual stress relief causing part deformation
node.main_point: Removing large amounts of material from stock with internal residual stresses can release those stresses and cause the workpiece to deform when it is unclamped.
node.source_quote: If you remove large parts of it, the stresses that were canceled out by say, two outer surfaces pulling with equal strength against the central bulk pushing, will result in the workpiece ending as soon as you unlatch it.

node.subject: thermal expansion impact on fits
node.main_point: Temperature differences or changes can alter dimensions via thermal expansion, turning an acceptable fit into interference or excessive clearance; ensure both mating parts are at similar and appropriate temperatures when designing or assembling close-tolerance fits.
node.source_quote: In these circumstances, one must ensure temperatures are uniform for both parts. If the parts were machined in 65b0F conditions, those parts might not fit together in colder or warmer conditions.

node.subject: router cutting reaction torque
node.main_point: Cutting with a rotating router bit generates a reaction torque on the machine, and the system must be able to resist that torque during operation.
node.source_quote: I.e as the material is removed a torsional moment (aka torque) develops. You'd need to be able to resist that.
node.example_context: CNC routing/milling with a rotating cutter

node.subject: allowing Poisson contraction in FEA constraints
node.main_point: A constraint scheme that permits Poisson-driven in‑plane contraction/expansion provides adequate restraint while avoiding artificial stresses. With the same mesh, allowing these DOFs yields more reasonable stress results.
node.source_quote: That should provide adequate fixture to the model (I hope I am not forgetting a dof), and it will also let the model contract/expand due to the Poisson ratio. For the same mesh you should see more reasonable results.

node.subject: reliance on bolt pattern precision
node.main_point: Designs that depend on bolt-hole precision to center rotating equipment will fail because such perfection is unattainable; use alignment methods instead.
node.source_quote: You will never attain the degree of perfection required to count on a bolt pattern to mate two pieces of rotation equipment.

backfills.backfill_answer: For CNC-milled aluminum, unsupported walls should be t ≥ 0.8–1.0 mm with height-to-thickness ratio H/t ≤ 8–10; for steels, use t ≥ 1.2–1.5 mm and H/t ≤ 6–8 to limit chatter and deflection. For thin plates during face-milling, keep clamp or vacuum support pitch to span ratio L/t ≤ 50 for aluminum and ≤ 30–40 for steels; add ribs or temporary tabs if larger spans are unavoidable. Aim for tool engagement ≤ 50% of wall height per pass and use small axial step-downs (≤ 0.5–1.0 t) to control bending. If tighter flatness (<0.1 mm per 300 mm) is required, plan semi-finish/relax/finish with symmetric material removal on both sides.

backfills.gap: No data on wax workholding for metals or polymers (strength, temperature sensitivity, residue) beyond epoxy tradeoffs.
backfills.backfill_answer: Fixturing waxes typically provide shear strength on the order of 2–6 MPa at 20–25°C; limit cutting side loads so average interface shear stays below ~1–2 MPa with a 2–3× safety factor and maximize bonded area. Most waxes soften markedly above 55–70°C; keep tool, coolant, and part temperatures below 45–50°C (light cuts, sharp tools, flood/mist) and allow 5–10 minutes to cool/solidify before heavy passes. Use shallow axial DOC (≤ 0.5–1.0 mm) and high rpm/low chip load to reduce torque; add shallow pockets or masking tape to increase mechanical keying on smooth metals. Removal usually requires mild heat (60–70°C) and mineral spirits/citrus solvent; verify compatibility with polymers (risk of stress cracking) and consult the specific product datasheet for exact strength and melt range.

frame_details.subject: minimum feature size DRC in planar mill CAM
frame_details.main_point: Planar-milling CAM software typically includes a minimum feature-size design rule check that can automatically remove thin copper slivers. Using this DRC can prevent leftover shavings during PCB milling.
frame_details.source_quote: Any good planar mill CAM program will have a design rule check for minimum feature size, and should be able to remove such slivers automatically. Worth checking into it.
frame_details.example_context: planar mill CAM for PCB isolation routing
frame_details.author: Kuba hasn't forgotten Monica

frame_details.subject: service-condition fit testing
frame_details.main_point: Test the fit under realistic service conditions, not just at standard lab conditions. A part that measures perfectly at around 1 atm and 20 C can still fail in its actual operating environment.
frame_details.source_quote: The simplest answer is already given test...you can manufacture it to perfection at 1 atm air pressure and 20 Celsius just to fail where it should be used...
frame_details.example_value: A fit verified at 1 atm and 20 C may not hold in the intended use environment.
frame_details.author: Patrik

frame_details.subject: reliance on bolt pattern precision
frame_details.main_point: Designs that depend on bolt-hole precision to center rotating equipment will fail because such perfection is unattainable; use alignment methods instead.
frame_details.source_quote: You will never attain the degree of perfection required to count on a bolt pattern to mate two pieces of rotation equipment.
frame_details.author: Chuck

frame_details.subject: epoxy filler adhesion vs removability tradeoff
frame_details.main_point: Using epoxy or similar resins as a temporary filler presents a tradeoff: if they adhere well, removal is difficult; if a release agent is used, they won’t adhere and must be mechanically retained.
frame_details.source_quote: The problem with epoxies or similar resins is that it will either adhere and be hard to remove or id you use a release agent it won't adhere at all unless it is held in by other means.
frame_details.author: Chris Johns

frame_details.subject: residual stresses from machining
frame_details.main_point: Machining induces deformation in the workpiece that leaves residual stresses concentrated near the surface of the part.
frame_details.source_quote: Machining a metal part will create residual stresses on its surface due to the deformation that the process introduces to it
frame_details.author: user3408085

frame_details.subject: too shallow depth of cut causing burnishing
frame_details.main_point: If the depth of cut is reduced too much, the tool may stop cutting and instead burnish the surface, leading to poor material removal and finish.
frame_details.source_quote: You run the risk of lowering the cut depth to the point where your tooling starts to burnish the workpiece and no longer cut the material.
frame_details.author: Pekka

frame_details.subject: residual stress relief causing part deformation
frame_details.main_point: Removing large amounts of material from stock with internal residual stresses can release those stresses and cause the workpiece to deform when it is unclamped.
frame_details.source_quote: If you remove large parts of it, the stresses that were canceled out by say, two outer surfaces pulling with equal strength against the central bulk pushing, will result in the workpiece ending as soon as you unlatch it.
frame_details.author: SF.

frame_details.subject: thermal expansion impact on fits
frame_details.main_point: Temperature differences or changes can alter dimensions via thermal expansion, turning an acceptable fit into interference or excessive clearance; ensure both mating parts are at similar and appropriate temperatures when designing or assembling close-tolerance fits.
frame_details.source_quote: In these circumstances, one must ensure temperatures are uniform for both parts. If the parts were machined in 65b0F conditions, those parts might not fit together in colder or warmer conditions.
frame_details.author: fred_dot_u

frame_details.subject: residual stresses from CNC milling
frame_details.main_point: CNC milling induces residual stresses in metal parts. Machining the material is asserted to leave internal stress in the workpiece.
frame_details.source_quote: CNC milling causes residual stresses in metals.
frame_details.author: Ron

frame_details.subject: vacuum hold-down using holes in fixture pocket
frame_details.main_point: If your workpiece sits in a pocket, you can add holes through the pocket’s base and attach a vacuum source (like a vacuum cleaner) to hold the part down instead of using mechanical clamps or tape.
frame_details.source_quote: As you have the "pocket" already, one method would be to have holes in the pocket base and use a vacuum cleaner to "suck" the piece down.
frame_details.example_value: Use the existing pocket and connect a household vacuum cleaner to holes in the pocket base to pull the wooden piece down during milling.
frame_details.example_context: CNC milling small wood parts located in a pocket; using a vacuum cleaner as the vacuum source for hold-down.
frame_details.author: Solar Mike

frame_details.subject: router cutting reaction torque
frame_details.main_point: Cutting with a rotating router bit generates a reaction torque on the machine, and the system must be able to resist that torque during operation.
frame_details.source_quote: I.e as the material is removed a torsional moment (aka torque) develops. You'd need to be able to resist that.
frame_details.example_context: CNC routing/milling with a rotating cutter
frame_details.author: NMech

frame_details.subject: machining-induced resonance from excitation frequency
frame_details.main_point: Vibration and chatter can occur when the cutting/excitation frequency aligns with the system’s natural frequency, leading to resonance and oscillations. This is a dynamics issue rather than a simple tool-wear problem.
frame_details.source_quote: it might be  that you are operating at a frequency which favours resonance  and oscillations.
frame_details.author: NMech

frame_details.subject: thermal methods for assembling interference fits
frame_details.main_point: Use thermal methods for assembling interference fits: heat the bearing or cool the shaft before assembly. The induced expansion or contraction provides temporary clearance to slip components together.
frame_details.source_quote: Standard practice is to heat the bearing with a bearing heater, or cool the shaft, prior to assembly. The thermal expansion (or contraction) allows just enough clearance for assembly.
frame_details.author: jko

frame_details.subject: simply supported beam point-load deflection
frame_details.main_point: For the simply supported case under a point load, the maximum deflection is δ_max = (P·L^3)/(48·E·I).
frame_details.source_quote:
for the 
simply supported case

(which is more likely what you will use):

$$\delta_{max} = \frac{P\cdot L^3}{48 \cdot E\cdot I}$$
frame_details.author: NMech

frame_details.subject: thermal assembly of interference fits by cooling
frame_details.main_point: You can assemble an interference fit without hammering by cooling the tube to take advantage of thermal contraction; the required temperature drop depends on the materials coefficient of thermal expansion.
frame_details.source_quote: There is also cooling which you would require to fit the tube without hammer for coefficient of thermal expansion 11e-6 K^{-1} (minimum same temperature fitting force could be calculated using radial contact stress, coefficient of friction and contact area):
frame_details.example_value: Using b1 3 11d710^-6 K^-1 (typical of steel), cooling the tube provides the clearance needed for slip-fit assembly.
frame_details.example_context: Steel or similar metals with coefficient of thermal expansion around 11d710^-6 K^-1.
frame_details.author: Tomáš Létal

frame_details.subject: double-stick tape workholding and heat-assisted release for CFRP
frame_details.main_point: Double‑stick carpet tape is a common way to hold small carbon‑fiber composite parts; releasing the tape may require heat, which the composite can tolerate provided the epoxy is not overheated.
frame_details.source_quote: Double stick carpet tape is a common substance and may require heating to remove without breaking the part, but carbon fiber composite can handle temperatures well enough as long as the epoxy resin is not damaged.
frame_details.example_context: Workholding thin carbon‑fiber composite parts on a sacrificial board
frame_details.author: fred_dot_u

frame_details.subject: too-light cut causing deflection and loss of bite
frame_details.main_point: If the cut is too light, elastic deflection of the workpiece (and potentially the tool) under cutting pressure can prevent the cutting edge from biting, so material isn’t removed as intended.
frame_details.source_quote: Materials have spring to them so taking too light a can cause the material to deform (I'm talking about the workpiece here but I suppose it also holds for the cutting tool) under cutting pressure and not "bite" preventing a proper cut from happening.
frame_details.author: DKNguyen

frame_details.subject: double-sided tape for temporary workholding
frame_details.main_point: Double-sided tape introduces compliance that allows parts to shift, making it unsuitable for precise routing operations, and it can leave adhesive residue on the workpiece.
frame_details.source_quote: - Two sided tape is thick and squishy (has some play, no good esp. on a router), leaves residue.
frame_details.example_context: woodworking routing operations where pieces are temporarily bonded face-to-face
frame_details.author: Jason C

frame_details.subject: double-sided tape creep and residue in fixturing
frame_details.main_point: Using double-sided/carpet tape for temporary wood fixturing can creep under continuous load, particularly in warm conditions, and may leave adhesive residue on the workpiece.
frame_details.source_quote: Many people have relied on types of double-sided tape, carpet tape being particularly favoured for its strong hold, for this sort of job for many years, but the hold can tend to creep with continual strain especially during warmer weather. And as you also mention it can leave a bothersome residue on the wood.
frame_details.example_context: Woodworking workholding using double-sided/carpet tape
frame_details.author: Graphus

frame_details.subject: adhesive layer thickness and creep (tape + CA method)
frame_details.main_point: Masking tape avoids residue on wood, and because the CA glue layer in the tape-to-tape method is very thin, the joint is less prone to creep under load.
frame_details.source_quote: Masking tape is of course purpose-made not to leave residue and the thinner glue layer means it's less subject to creep.
frame_details.example_context: Woodworking temporary bonding using masking tape and CA glue
frame_details.author: Graphus

frame_details.subject: performance of tape-to-tape CA joint
frame_details.main_point: A tape-to-tape CA bond provides a strong, rigid hold during machining, yet the parts can be separated with light prying and the masking tape removes cleanly afterward.
frame_details.source_quote: And the hold of the superglue is very strong and rigid, but despite this you can pop the two pieces apart with minimal prying. The masking tape then peels from the wood with ease.
frame_details.example_context: Woodworking temporary fixturing with masking tape and CA glue
frame_details.author: Graphus
